meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Mineral and Power Resources
meta.intro: Detailed Class 8 Geography notes on minerals, their types, distribution, extraction, uses, conservation, and conventional as well as non-conventional power resources.

objectives: Define mineral and distinguish it from rock and ore.
Classify minerals into metallic (ferrous and non-ferrous) and non-metallic types.
Explain the methods of mineral extraction: mining, drilling and quarrying.
Describe the distribution of major minerals in the world and in India.
List important uses of minerals and explain why conservation is necessary.
Distinguish conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.
Describe coal, petroleum, natural gas and hydel power as conventional sources.
Explain solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, tidal and biogas energy as non-conventional sources.

blocks.text: A mineral is a naturally occurring substance that has a definite chemical composition. Minerals are formed by natural processes under different geological conditions and are not distributed evenly across the Earth. They are concentrated in particular rock formations and areas.
A naturally occurring substance that has a definite chemical composition.
An aggregate of one or more minerals. Rocks do not have a fixed chemical composition of their constituent minerals.
A rock from which minerals can be profitably extracted.

Minerals can be identified by physical properties such as colour, density, hardness and lustre, and by chemical properties such as solubility. They form the basis of modern industry and are essential for economic development.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Minerals take thousands to millions of years to form. Once extracted and used, they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime. This makes them non-renewable resources.
On the basis of composition, minerals are broadly classified into metallic and non-metallic minerals.
1. Metallic Minerals
Metallic minerals contain metal in raw form. Metals are hard, lustrous substances that conduct heat and electricity.

items: Examples: iron ore, bauxite, manganese ore, copper, gold, silver, lead.
Metallic minerals are further divided into ferrous and non-ferrous minerals.

blocks.text: Metallic minerals that contain iron. Examples: iron ore, manganese, chromite.
Metallic minerals that do not contain iron. Examples: gold, silver, copper, lead, bauxite, tin.
2. Non-metallic Minerals
Non-metallic minerals do not contain metals. They include both industrial minerals and mineral fuels.

items: Examples: limestone, mica, gypsum, salt, coal, petroleum, natural gas.
Mineral fuels such as coal and petroleum are also grouped under non-metallic minerals.

blocks.title: Where different minerals occur
blocks.text: Metallic minerals are generally found in igneous and metamorphic rocks that form large plateaus. Non-metallic minerals are commonly found in sedimentary rock formations of plains and young fold mountains.
Minerals are extracted from the Earth’s crust by different methods depending on their depth and nature.
The process of taking out minerals from rocks buried under the Earth’s surface.

items: Open-cast mining: Minerals lying at shallow depths are taken out by removing the surface layer.
Shaft mining: Deep vertical shafts are dug to reach mineral deposits that lie far below the surface.

blocks.text: Deep wells are bored to extract minerals such as petroleum and natural gas.
Minerals that lie very close to the surface are simply dug out.

blocks.title: Important Point
blocks.text: The method of extraction depends on the depth of the deposit, the type of mineral and the economic cost of recovering it.
Minerals are unevenly distributed across the world and within countries. Their occurrence depends on geological history and rock type.
World Distribution (Selected Highlights)

items: Asia: China and India have large iron-ore deposits. China, Malaysia and Indonesia are major tin producers. China also leads in lead, antimony and tungsten.
Europe: Leading producer of iron ore (Russia, Ukraine, Sweden, France). Copper, lead, zinc, manganese and nickel deposits occur in eastern Europe and European Russia.
North America: Canadian Shield (iron, nickel, gold, uranium, copper); Appalachian region (coal); western mountain ranges (copper, lead, zinc, gold, silver).
South America: Brazil (iron ore), Chile and Peru (copper), Brazil and Bolivia (tin). Also rich in gold, silver, zinc, manganese, bauxite and diamonds.
Africa: World’s largest producer of diamonds, gold and platinum. Gold in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Democratic Republic of Congo; oil in Nigeria, Libya and Angola.
Australia: Largest producer of bauxite. Leading producer of gold, diamond, iron ore, tin and nickel. Kalgoorlie and Coolgardie are famous gold areas.
Antarctica: Possible deposits of coal, iron, gold, silver and oil, but commercial mining is restricted.

blocks.text: Distribution in India

rows: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Goa, Maharashtra, Karnataka

blocks.text: Uses of Minerals

items: Jewellery: gold, silver, platinum and gemstones.
Coins, electrical wires and pipes: copper.
Computer industry: silicon obtained from quartz.
Automobiles, aeroplanes, buildings and cookware: aluminium obtained from bauxite.
Iron and steel industry: iron ore and manganese.
Cement and construction: limestone.
Electrical industry: mica.

blocks.text: Why Conserve Minerals?
Minerals are non-renewable. Their formation takes thousands to millions of years, while human consumption is extremely rapid. Once exhausted, they cannot be replaced within a human time-scale.

items: Reduce wastage during mining and processing.
Recycle metals whenever possible.
Use substitutes and improve technology to extract more from lower-grade ores.
Practise the 3Rs – Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.

blocks.title: Key Idea
blocks.text: Conservation of minerals is essential for sustainable industrial development and for leaving resources for future generations.
Power (energy) is required for industry, agriculture, transport, communication, defence and everyday life. Power resources are broadly classified into conventional and non-conventional sources.
Sources that have been in common use for a long time (firewood, fossil fuels and hydel power).
Newer, alternative sources developed because conventional sources are limited and polluting (solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, tidal, biogas).
1. Firewood
Widely used for cooking and heating, especially in rural areas. In India, more than half of the energy used by villagers still comes from firewood. Overuse leads to deforestation.
2. Fossil Fuels
Fossil fuels are formed from the remains of plants and animals buried under the Earth for millions of years and converted by heat and pressure. They are limited and non-renewable.

The most abundant fossil fuel, formed from giant ferns and swamps buried millions of years ago (often called ‘buried sunshine’). Used as domestic fuel, in iron and steel industry and to generate thermal power.
Major world producers: China, USA, Germany, Russia, South Africa. In India: Raniganj, Jharia, Dhanbad and Bokaro (Jharkhand).
A thick black liquid found between layers of rocks. Called ‘black gold’ because of its high value. Refined to produce petrol, diesel, kerosene, wax, plastics and lubricants.
Major world producers: Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, USA, Russia, Venezuela. In India: Digboi (Assam), Mumbai High, Krishna-Godavari delta.
Usually found with petroleum deposits. Used as domestic and industrial fuel. Cleaner than coal and oil.
In India found in Jaisalmer, Krishna-Godavari delta, Tripura and offshore Mumbai.
3. Hydel Power
Electricity generated by the force of falling water. River water stored in dams is made to fall from a height over turbine blades, which turn generators.

items: About one-fourth of the world’s electricity is produced from hydel power.
Advantages: non-polluting, renewable, multipurpose (irrigation, flood control).
Important projects in India: Bhakra Nangal, Gandhi Sagar, Nagarjuna Sagar, Damodar Valley.

blocks.title: Caution
blocks.text: Fossil fuels are being consumed much faster than they can form. Burning them also causes air pollution and climate change. Their use must be carefully managed.
Because fossil fuels are limited and polluting, alternative sources are being developed. These are generally cleaner and more sustainable.
Solar Energy

Energy from the Sun captured by solar cells and panels. Used for heating, lighting, solar cookers, solar dryers, traffic signals and community lighting. Especially useful in tropical countries with abundant sunshine.
Wind Energy

High-speed winds turn windmills connected to generators. Wind farms (clusters of windmills) are located in coastal regions and mountain passes. Major users: Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, USA, Spain, India.
Nuclear Energy

Obtained from the energy stored in the nuclei of atoms of radioactive elements such as uranium and thorium through nuclear fission. India has nuclear power stations at Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata (Rajasthan), Narora (Uttar Pradesh) and Kaiga (Karnataka). Thorium is abundant in the monazite sands of Kerala.
Geothermal Energy

Heat energy from the Earth’s interior. Temperature increases with depth. Sometimes the heat reaches the surface as hot springs. Used to generate electricity in places where geothermal activity is strong.
Tidal Energy
Energy generated from the rise and fall of tides. Dams are built across narrow openings of the sea. The movement of water during high and low tides turns turbines.
Biogas

A gaseous fuel produced by the decomposition of organic waste (animal dung, plant material, kitchen waste) in the absence of oxygen. Clean, renewable and useful for cooking and lighting, especially in rural areas.

blocks.title: Chapter Takeaway
blocks.text: Minerals and power resources form the backbone of modern economy. Because most minerals and fossil fuels are non-renewable, careful extraction, recycling and a shift towards cleaner non-conventional energy sources are essential for sustainable development.

takeaways: A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a definite chemical composition; an ore is a rock from which it can be profitably extracted.
Minerals are classified as metallic (ferrous and non-ferrous) and non-metallic.
Extraction methods include open-cast mining, shaft mining, drilling and quarrying.
Minerals are unevenly distributed; India is rich in iron ore, bauxite, mica and salt.
Minerals are non-renewable and must be conserved by reducing waste and recycling.
Conventional energy sources include firewood, coal, petroleum, natural gas and hydel power.
Non-conventional sources include solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, tidal and biogas energy.
A shift towards cleaner, renewable energy is necessary for sustainable development.
revision.summary: Minerals are naturally occurring substances with definite chemical composition. They are classified as metallic (ferrous and non-ferrous) and non-metallic. Extraction is done by mining, drilling or quarrying. Distribution is highly uneven both globally and within India. Because minerals take a very long time to form, conservation through reduced wastage and recycling is essential. Power resources are divided into conventional (firewood, fossil fuels, hydel) and non-conventional (solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, tidal, biogas) sources. Growing energy demand and environmental concerns make the development of non-conventional sources increasingly important.

questions.why: Limestone does not contain metal and is classified as non-metallic.

questions.why: Because of their high economic value, petroleum products are called black gold.

questions.q: Electricity generated from coal is known as:
questions.why: Thermal power stations burn coal to produce electricity.

questions.why: Wind energy is a modern alternative source and is classified as non-conventional.

questions.q: Which method is used to extract petroleum?
questions.why: Petroleum is extracted by drilling deep wells into oil-bearing rocks.

questions.q: Which continent is the largest producer of diamonds, gold and platinum?
questions.why: Africa is the world’s leading producer of these three minerals.
Biogas is formed by the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter such as dung and plant waste.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of hydel power?

options: They form very slowly over geological time
